title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 The Norton Guide to AI-Aware Teaching
author: Marc Watkins
summary: Marc Watkins argues that AI is not merely a problem for education to manage but the richest subject for 'provocative pedagogy' a generation has seen -- contested, consequential, ethically tangled, and evolving weekly. Co-authoring The Norton Guide to AI-Aware Teaching with Annette Vee and Derek Bruff, Watkins centers human agency in faculty and student choices around machine intelligence. He distinguishes between 'engaging' AI (critically examining it as a subject) and 'adopting' AI (unreflectively using it), arguing that critical discussions about AI use and impact are pedagogically valuable even without requiring students to use chatbots. The article surveys three institutional support models: communities of practice like UNT's Generative AI Institute for Teaching, embedded AI Guides programs like UVA's, and wholesale course redesign initiatives like Yale's, which funds courses that explore AI use, teach ethical issues, and redesign to curb AI's influence. Watkins ends with a list of topics suitable for classroom discussion and two interactive AI-built workshops educators can adapt.
points: * AI is 'the subject of provocative pedagogy' -- contested, consequential, and ethically tangled -- making it among the richest instructional subjects available to educators today, not just a compliance problem to solve. * Engaging AI critically as a curriculum subject is distinct from adopting AI as a tool; students can learn profoundly about AI through discussion and analysis without using a chatbot themselves. * Three faculty support models are gaining traction: funded communities of practice (UNT), embedded department-level AI Guides (UVA), and wholesale course redesign with ethical and pedagogical scope (Yale). * Yale's AI course redesign pilot stands out for funding three distinct approaches: exploring AI in the classroom, teaching students about AI's ethical issues, and redesigning teaching to curb AI's influence -- all simultaneously. * Educators can begin small with a single conversation using AI as a divisive topic, or use tools like Claude Cowork to vibe-code interactive workshops -- the key is intentional, human-centered engagement.
quotes: Teaching about AI and its impact on our culture makes for some of the best teaching material in a generation. AI is the subject of provocative pedagogy. It is contested, consequential, ethically tangled, and changing weekly.

Engaging AI isn't adopting AI. Having critical and thoughtful discussions with students about their AI use and AI's impact on their community can create the type of creative and curious responses for students to learn about this technology without asking them to use a chatbot.
The purpose of our guide is to center human agency in choices faculty and students make around machine intelligence.
If a teacher does ask students to use AI, then it should be intentional and aligned with course learning outcomes, depending on your AI stance and overall policies for the class.
There are opportunities to engage AI in all of our classes, and no, by engage AI I don't mean use or adopt AI.
